name: Moscow
info: Moscow is a city on the Moskva River in Central Russia, first documented in 1147, which grew from a minor border town into the capital of the Grand Principality of Moscow, the Tsardom of Russia, the Soviet Union and the Russian Federation.

facts.founded: First documented in 1147, as a meeting place of Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich. Its first prince was Daniel, a son of Alexander Nevsky, who received it as hereditary land in 1263.
facts.where: On the banks of the Moskva River on the East European Plain in Central Russia, in the present-day Russian Federation.
facts.known: The Kremlin and Red Square; the rise of Muscovy under Ivan III; the doctrine of Moscow as the Third Rome; the burning of the city by the Crimean Tatars in 1571; the fire of 1812; capital of the Soviet Union; the Moscow Metro; the Battle of Moscow
facts.today: Moscow is the capital and largest city of the Russian Federation and is governed as a federal city.

t: Moscow was a minor border town when it was first recorded in 1147, and it rose under Daniel's descendants, who collected tribute for the khan of the Golden Horde and drew the seat of the Russian Church to the city.

Ivan III united nearly all the Russian states with Moscow and rebuilt the Kremlin, and in 1547 Ivan the Terrible was crowned there as the first tsar of all Russia, but Peter the Great moved his government to Saint Petersburg in 1712.
Moscow became the capital again in 1918 under Lenin, grew through the Soviet period, held back the German army in 1941 and 1942, and remained the capital of the Russian Federation after 1991.
dyk: In 1937 letters were written to the Central Committee of the Communist Party proposing that Moscow be renamed "Stalindar" or "Stalinodar". Stalin rejected the suggestion.

sections.origins:
Moscow stands on the Moskva River in Central Russia, on the East European Plain. The site has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Among the earliest finds are relics of the Lyalovo culture, which experts assign to the Neolithic and which show that the first inhabitants were hunters and gatherers. The Neolithic Schukinskaya site on the Moscow River is the oldest evidence, and there is also a burial ground of the Fatyanovskaya culture and an Iron Age settlement of the Dyakovo culture on the territory of the Kremlin. The Finnic Merya and Muroma were among the pre-Slavic tribes of the area, and around 950 CE the Slavic Vyatichi and Krivichi settled there; the Vyatichi may have formed the majority of the indigenous population.

The city's name is thought to come from that of the river. The best-grounded theory derives it from a Proto-Balto-Slavic root related to "wet", so that Moskva may mean a river at a wetland or marsh. A Finno-Ugric hypothesis holds that the Merya and Muroma called the river Mustajoki, "Black River". Moscow is first mentioned in the chronicles in 1147, as a meeting place of Yuri Dolgorukiy and Sviatoslav Olgovich, when it was a minor town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal. It became a fortified gorod in the 1150s, when the first walls of the Kremlin were built. Yuri Dolgorukiy is also said to have fortified it in 1156 with a timber fence and a moat.
sections.growth:
Moscow's importance increased during the second half of the 12th century, but its rise began after Daniel, the youngest son of Alexander Nevsky, received it in 1263. After Daniel's death in 1303 the territory of the principality almost tripled, and it then covered the whole of the Moskva River and its tributaries, which made Moscow self-sufficient and gave it a river network for trade. Ivan I used the tribute he collected for the khan to develop the city. The metropolitan of the Russian Church moved his seat there from Vladimir, and the foundation of the Dormition Cathedral, the first stone church of Moscow, was laid in 1326. The limestone walls and towers of the Kremlin were built in 1366 to 1368, and a distinct architectural school emerged in the late 14th century.

Under Ivan III, who became Grand Prince in 1462, Moscow was reshaped as the capital of a growing state. By 1500 it had a population of 100,000 and was one of the largest cities in the world. Ivan invited architects from Renaissance Italy to rebuild the Kremlin, among them Petrus Antonius Solarius, who designed the walls and towers completed in 1495, and Marco Ruffo, who designed the new palace. The Ivan the Great Bell Tower was built in 1505 to 1508, and the Red Square appeared as the "Hollow Field". In the first half of the 17th century the population doubled from 100,000 to 200,000. After 1750 it grew tenfold, reaching 1.8 million by 1915.
sections.rulers:
Moscow began as a town on the western border of the principality of Rostov-Suzdal, which emerged from the disintegration of Kievan Rus'. Its first prince, Daniel, ruled from the 1260s, and his descendants ruled as princes and then as grand princes. They struggled with the princes of Tver over the grand principality; Yury won recognition from the khan in 1318 but lost it four years later, and Ivan I recovered it. The khan of the Golden Horde at first backed Moscow against the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and also meddled to keep it from growing too strong. After 1389 the thrones of Vladimir and Moscow were permanently united. During the reign of Vasily II a civil war began in 1425 and Moscow changed hands numerous times; it ended in 1450. Ivan III's defeat of the Tatars in 1480 traditionally marks the end of Tatar suzerainty, and nearly all the Russian states were united with Moscow in his reign.

In 1547 Ivan the Terrible was crowned in Moscow as the first tsar of all Russia. From 1610 to 1612 troops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth occupied it, and in 1613 the Zemsky Sobor elected Michael Romanov tsar. In 1712 Peter the Great moved his government to Saint Petersburg, though the capital returned to Moscow for a time from 1728 to 1732. Lenin moved the capital back on 12 March 1918, and Moscow was the capital of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1991 and then of the Russian Federation.
sections.life:
Moscow grew around the Kremlin, and in the 16th and 17th centuries it developed in concentric divisions once separated by walls: the Kremlin, Kitay-gorod, the White City, the Earthen City and the settlements outside the walls. Houses were built of pine and spruce logs, and the city's appearance had not changed much by the 18th century. The settlements outside the ramparts included the Meshchanskaya sloboda, where by 1682 692 households of Ukrainians and Belarusians abducted from their hometowns in the Russo-Polish War of 1654 to 1667 had been established. Moscow was the centre of Russian Orthodoxy, and before 1917 it was called the city of "40 times 40 churches". In 1441 Vasily II arrested the metropolitan for signing the Council of Florence, seven years later the Russian bishops elected their own metropolitan, which amounted to a declaration of autocephaly, and in 1492 the Russian metropolitan called Moscow an imperial city for the first time. The doctrine of Moscow as the "Third Rome" continued to develop in the reign of Vasily III.

Moscow State University was founded in 1755, and the newspaper Moskovskiye Vedomosti appeared in 1756. The Mytischinskiy water pipeline, the first in Russia, was built between 1781 and 1804. The railway between Moscow and Saint Petersburg began operating in 1851, after which Moscow served as the central railway hub of Russia. In 1905 Alexander Adrianov became the first official mayor. The Moscow Metro opened in 1935, with the artwork of its 13 original stations, and postwar housing was solved with prefabricated high-rise blocks.
sections.crises:
During the Mongol invasions of 1237 to 1238 Moscow was sacked, and the Golden Horde is also said to have burned the city to the ground and killed its inhabitants. The Black Death reached Moscow in 1353 and killed the ruler Simeon, his sons and the metropolitan. Two fires in 1547 destroyed much of the town. In 1571 the Crimean Tatars, supported by the Ottomans, captured and burned it, leaving only the Kremlin; the annals record that only 30,000 of 200,000 inhabitants survived. New walls built between 1584 and 1591 held them back when they attacked again in 1591. The famine of 1601 to 1603 killed possibly 100,000 people in Moscow. Plague epidemics struck in 1570 to 1571, 1592 and 1654 to 1656, and the plague killed more than 80% of the population in 1654 to 1655. Fires burned down much of the wooden city in 1626 and 1648, and the Russian plague of 1770 to 1772 killed up to 100,000.

When Napoleon invaded in 1812 the Muscovites were evacuated. The fire that followed is attributed principally to Russian sabotage, though it is also described as only suspected to have begun that way. An estimated three-quarters of the city lay in ruin; a Commission for the Construction of the City of Moscow was set up in 1813 to rebuild it. In 1941 the German Army Group Centre was stopped at the outskirts, and the city was declared under siege from 20 October. Casualties from 30 September 1941 to 7 January 1942 are estimated at 248,000 to 400,000 for the Wehrmacht and 650,000 to 1,280,000 for the Red Army.
sections.legacy:
The Kremlin and Red Square, built between the 14th and 17th centuries, are among the UNESCO World Heritage Sites of the city, and so is the Church of the Ascension at Kolomenskoye, which dates from 1532. Saint Basil's Cathedral and the Ivan the Great Bell Tower are older landmarks. The city's layout, with its radial roads and rings, follows the lines of its medieval walls: the Boulevard Ring lies on the 16th-century wall of the White City, and the Garden Ring marks the limits set by the ramparts of 1592. The Seven Sisters, the Stalinist skyscrapers, and the constructivist work of the early Soviet years, such as Lenin's Mausoleum and the Shukhov Tower, belong to the 20th century.

The Soviet period also destroyed much. The tradition of preserving cultural heritage was broken, independent preservation societies were disbanded by the end of the 1920s, and the destruction of churches peaked around 1932. Stalin's broad avenues took many historical buildings, among them the Sukharev Tower, and the Kazan Cathedral and the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour were destroyed and later rebuilt in the 1990s. Of the 50 churches operating in 1959, 30 were closed and six demolished under Khrushchev. In 1965 Moscow was given the title of Hero City. It was the capital of the Russian Federation from 1991, and in 2012 its area more than doubled when it expanded southwest into the Moscow Oblast.

summary: Moscow, on the Moskva River in Central Russia, was first recorded in 1147 and rose under the princes who collected tribute for the Golden Horde. It became the capital of Muscovy, the Tsardom and, from 1918, the Soviet Union, and it is the capital of the Russian Federation.
references: Robert O. Crummey, The Formation of Muscovy 1300 - 1613 (Routledge, 2014)
John Fennell, The Emergence of Moscow, 1304–1359 (University of California Press, 2023)
notes: START: first documented 1147; no founding date or founder is given. Both articles agree on 1147.

I used 1263 and 'from the 1260s'; the monastery date is left out because the main article says it was founded on the right bank without a date.

FORTIFICATION: main says the first Kremlin walls were built in the 1150s; history says Yuri fortified it in 1156. Both given, the second attributed to the history article. I wrote 'the history article' in a few places; the editor may want to turn these into neutral wording.

1238: main says Moscow was 'sacked following the destruction of Ryazan'; history says the Horde 'burned the city to the ground and killed its inhabitants'. Event label uses 'burn' (history); the section gives both. The event year 1238 vs the invasion span 1237-1238.

1812 FIRE: main says 'principally the effect of Russian sabotage'; history says it is 'suspected' to have started so. Disputed; I attributed the stronger claim to the main article. 'three-quarters in ruins' is from the history article only.

BATTLE OF MOSCOW: main says the German army was stopped between October 1941 and January 1942; history says 6 December 1941. I gave the casualty estimates (main only) and the siege date of 20 October (both).
PLAGUE: main gives epidemics in 1570-1571, 1592 and 1654-1656 and the 80% figure for 1654-1655; history says 1654-55. Used main's.
POPULATION 1500: 100,000 is from the history article only. 'Third Rome' doctrine in Vasily III's reign is from the main article; Ivan III's territorial figures omitted.

CAPITAL 1712: both give 1712; the history article also mentions a 1728-1732 return of the capital under the Supreme Privy Council. The main article says only 'in 1712 moved his government', and its intro says 1712 too. Left a single mention of 1728-1732 from the history article.
